payload.query: What did Parliament discuss about healthcare delivery and public health services?

topk.text: Mr Speaker, you would recollect that in the previous Parliament, which is the Seventh Parliament, Leadership, together with the PSB, took a decision that former Hon Members of Parliament could visit our clinic, but if there were prescriptions they have to buy, then they would go outside to buy. If we look at the predicament of most of our Hon Colleagues— I always say that they were like us yesterday; tomorrow, we would be like them. If we do not work hard to improve, at least, the medical care of former Hon Members of Parliament, we would not be doing ourselves any good. I would like this House to consider that seriously, so that in the future, we would make adequate provisions to take care of — At least, there should be enough medication in the clinic. I know we would not be able to foot the bills of former Hon Members of Parliament if they go out to buy a prescription and come back to make a claim. But, at least, if we have some critical medications in our clinic, they would be taken care of when they visit the clinic, and that will do us a lot of good. Mr Speaker, I know time is far spent and others may want to make some comments on the Budget Estimates of Parliament, but I must say this. I know it may be a little digression: The loss of one of our colleagues or brothers, Mr Paul Baka, whose body was brought to Parliament today. I was sad. I know many staff die, and we only talk about Hon Members of Parliament, but this is a gentleman who worked directly with this Chamber, and I remember that during the Post-Budget Workshop, he sat here throughout and even made the roll call. Unfortunately, he lost his life when he went home and did not wake up. Mr Speaker, we must know that it is not only Hon Members of Parliament who go through tremendous stress working here. It is the same with our staff, especially some categories of our staff. Until we close and go home, those who work directly with us are not able to go home. For some of them, even after we have closed, they still have to stay behind to prepare for the next day. I recollect very well that throughout my period in Leadership, this young man — 49 years may not be too young, but because of the advancement of medicine today, to die at 49 years, he died too young. Mr Speaker, we need to encourage the Clerk to Parliament to ensure that we make provisions for the health of our staff; it is so critical. This is because nobody takes care of other’s children today. Yes, we may all mourn and bid him farewell tomorrow, but what happens to his children, wife and family that he was taking care of? Mr Speaker, let us invest in the health of our staff, especially, the core ones. Mr Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to

Mr First Deputy Speaker: Hon Members, luckily the Minister for Health is here. We need not make any further direction to him. Minister for Health, may we hear you on the issue? Minister for Health (Mr Kwabena Mintah Akandoh) (MP): Mr Speaker, let me use this opportunity to thank the Parliamentary Select Committee on Health, together with all stakeholders, for the successful and fruitful deliberations this morning as far as this strike is concerned. Mr Speaker, the Ministry—[Laughter] Mr Speaker, the Ministry of Health is the mother Ministry for the nurses and midwives, and we will continue to behave like mothers for these nurses and midwives. Mr Speaker, let me assure you that out of the fruitful deliberations we had this morning, once the strike is called off, we are committed to engaging our nurses and midwives to arrive at mutually acceptable conditions, so that they will continue to do what they do best to contribute to the health care of this sector. Mr Speaker, I thank you for the opportunity. Mr First Deputy Speaker: Hon Members, that brings us to the end of that Statement. Hon Member, you have the floor. Mr First Deputy Speaker: Hon Minister, you have the floor. Minister for Health (Mr Kwabena Mintah Akandoh) (MP): Mr Speaker, I wish to thank the Hon Member for Sefwi Akontombra for his Question regarding the status of the Nsawora Health Centre. The Nsawora Health Centre, located in the Western North Region, was established to serve the health care needs of the people of Nsawora and its surrounding communities. As of the latest assessment conducted by the Regional Health Directorate, the physical infrastructure of the facility is approximately 80 per cent complete. Mr Speaker, on the issue of the registered nurses, the President directed that a meeting be convened by the relevant Ministers to address the concerns of the nurses. I was there when he gave the directive, because I went to report the work that Parliament did in terms of mediating to get the nurses to call off the strike and the promises that Parliament made to the nurses, and he directed that a meeting be held with him to see how far we can go in terms of meeting the needs of the nurses. Unfortunately, the Ministers are all out of town as indicated on radio yesterday by the Ranking Member for the Committee on Health. The Minister for Finance and the Minister for Health are all out with the President in Brussels on a major health issue. So, when they come back, I will follow up and ensure that that meeting to address the concerns of the registered nurses, as promised by Parliament, takes place so that we see how far we can reach out to the nurses. I believe the issues have been addressed. Thank you very much. Mr Speaker, in the last few days, we have witnessed the suffering of our people across the health centres, and I believe today's Committee meeting will 89 12th June, 2025 90 Statements hopefully bring to an end the sufferings of our people. But it also serves as a very stark reminder of the gamut of issues affecting the health sector. I strongly believe that instead of political apparatchiks and propagandists subjecting these nurses to abuse, insult and unfair and foul language, I think that the Health Ministry must also take steps to ensure that the issues raised by these nurses and those in the health sector are also not repeated. Mr Speaker, no one can anticipate a time of disaster, just like a fish caught in a cruel net or a bird caught in a wicked trap. We can be struck by illness on any day, and I want to believe that if there is one sector that we must also take seriously, it is the health sector. I want to commend the Committee's effort, but I also believe that the Minister for Health and the Ministry too must adopt measures that will be more embracing, and communicate better to our folks in the health sector. On this note, let me commend Dr Ayew, Hon Ahmed, the team and the Committee that also sat today together with our professionals from the health sector to bring this standoff to a close. Mr Afenyo-Markin: Mr Speaker, thank you for the opportunity to add my voice to this report. First, let me commend highly, our respected Colleague, Mr James Klutse Avedzi. This Public Accounts Committee started gaining prominence when former MPMr Silas Mensah, was then the Chairman. Then we had Mr Albert Kan-Dapaah also taking over and we had Mr Agyeman Manu, who later became an Hon Minister for Health, who 149 19th December, 2024 150 also took charge, and now we have Mr Avedzi. There is no doubt on my mind that he discharges his duty to the country with distinction;the way he had ensured that there is a non-partisan approach to the handling of the work. I watch him on Television; I was once upon a time a member of that Committee, and I know the industry he puts in his work. Mr Speaker, every now and then, we debate reports, but I have been wondering what else we can do beyond the debate. There is a constitutional provision, Article 187, which provides for the handling of this matter, but beyond the debate, these institutions of state who act against the regulations, what do we do to them? I think once upon a time, Mr Avedzi was even calling for the arrest of some officers and I had the opportunity to question him that that was not the right procedure. Of course, I said so; that was not the right procedure. It is like what I am telling your people who have formed a so called Committee called Operation Recover All Loot (O.R.A.L) to do a certain investigation. We do not know where that institution comes from and that was the very thing he was trying to do and I said no! Mr Speaker, I think Parliament must make a strong recommendation for the Office of the Attorney-General and Ministry of Justice to set up a unit specifically to handle the prosecution of such matters. The Police, and Economic and Organised Crime Office (EOCO), also have various units that handle certain offences. payload.answer: Parliament discussed healthcare delivery and public health services in relation to the strike by nurses and midwives. They expressed concern about the impact of the strike on patients and the quality of healthcare delivery [888e3eff0f49cdf77dfcb72ccd7c599961ba602e709f7dd74027846b9df447fe:57]. The Minister for Health, Mr Kwabena Mintah Akandoh, assured Parliament that the Ministry would continue to address the concerns of nurses and midwives [84e5026304f7c46d2154b7fbf6debd2d9a6a5b2deb5c1c9dfc48d67273faf5d6:37].
